title: The Elo rating
hook: A chess ranking made by a physics professor now ranks gamers, football teams and AI.
peek: Arpad Elo, a physics professor and strong chess player, designed a simple way to rate players from their results. Chess adopted it decades ago, and versions of it now rank online gamers, football teams and even AI chatbots.
lede: Arpad Elo was a Hungarian-born physics professor at Marquette University in Wisconsin and a strong chess player. He thought the existing chess rankings were unfair, so he designed a system based on statistics. The United States Chess Federation adopted it in 1960, and the world chess federation, FIDE, followed in 1970. It is a name, not an acronym, so it is Elo, not ELO.

bullets.text: Each rating predicts how a game should go. Beat someone rated much higher and you gain a lot of points, while beating someone much lower earns very few. A 400-point gap means the stronger player is expected to score about 90%.
Ratings give chess a simple league table across time. Magnus Carlsen reached 2882 in 2014, the highest classical rating anyone has achieved.
The same method is used to rate Go players, national football teams and players in many online games, where it helps match people of similar skill.
Researchers rank AI chatbots in public arenas where people compare two anonymous answers and pick the better one. The scores use Elo-style maths, treating each vote like a game won or lost.
